question:
Patient note:
A 23-year-old woman in her final year of veterinary school came to the student health center late this afternoon for a comprehensive review of the chronic conditions followed by several subspecialists before she begins a six-week rural externship with limited medical resources. She walked briskly from the bus stop carrying a 10-kg backpack of reference texts, reported no limitation when climbing the three flights to the clinic, and denied chest tightness, palpitations, exertional light-headedness, ankle swelling, episodic shortness of breath, claudication, or coldness of the toes. At age sixteen she developed symmetric pain and morning stiffness of the small joints of the hands accompanied by photosensitive facial erythema and had serologies notable for a high-titer antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA reactivity, and hypocomplementemia; since that time she has taken hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily with good control, needs only occasional naproxen for wrist flares during examination periods, and has never experienced nephrotic-range proteinuria, serositis, seizure, or cognitive change. Two years ago, after an intense round of equine obstetrics duty that required frequent non-steroidal analgesic use for back strain, she awoke with black, tarry stools and epigastric gnawing. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy the same day revealed a 1.2-cm clean-based ulcer on the anterior duodenal bulb and a rapid urease test positive for Helicobacter; she completed clarithromycin-based triple therapy and eight weeks of 40 mg pantoprazole daily, after which repeat endoscopy showed complete mucosal healing. She continues a maintenance proton-pump inhibitor each morning, has had no further melena, hematemesis, or iron-deficiency anemia, and avoids over-the-counter ibuprofen. During routine laboratory screening last summer her alanine aminotransferase was found to be mildly elevated at 62 U/L, with aspartate aminotransferase 55 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0; viral hepatitis serologies and ultrasound ruled out steatosis, mass, or biliary dilation, and a FibroScan recorded liver stiffness in the normal range. She drinks one glass of wine at weddings only, has no tattoos, and has never injected drugs. Follow-up chemistries two weeks ago remained stable—alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L—without jaundice, pedal edema, abdominal distention, or pruritus, and hepatology characterized her condition as early inflammatory change that warrants yearly monitoring but no pharmacotherapy at present. Endocrine review is unremarkable: she monitors her weight weekly because of family history of type 2 diabetes, logs fasting capillary glucose values between 85 mg/dL and 98 mg/dL, and the most recent hemoglobin A1c was 5.2 %. She eats mostly plant-based meals prepared in the dormitory communal kitchen, bicycles 40 minutes daily, and maintains a stable weight of 62 kg at a height of 172 cm (body-mass index 20.9 kg/m²). She has never smoked and limits caffeine to one morning coffee; she denies recreational drug use. Gynecologic history includes regular 30-day cycles and combined oral contraceptive use for dysmenorrhea without thromboembolic complications; she has never been pregnant. She is up to date on vaccines including human papillomavirus series and receives annual influenza immunization. There is no family record of premature coronary events, stroke, or hereditary clotting disorders; a maternal aunt has systemic lupus with renal involvement, and her father was treated for a perforated gastric ulcer in his thirties. Current medications consist of hydroxychloroquine, pantoprazole, a combined ethinyl estradiol–levonorgestrel pill, naproxen 220 mg as needed (taken less than once monthly), and a vitamin D supplement; she reports mild urticaria to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, unintentional weight change, dyspnea on talking, chronic cough, hemoptysis, headache, focal weakness, visual field loss, numbness, or easy bruising. After five minutes of seated rest her vitals read: temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 114/68 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. She appears well nourished, speaks in complete sentences, and is oriented to situation, date, and location. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist without ulcers. Neck is supple, thyroid non-enlarged, carotid upstrokes brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulse is 1 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. Cardiac examination reveals a nondisplaced apical impulse, crisp S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with symmetric excursion. Abdomen is flat, soft, nontender, with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, smooth and nontender, spleen is not felt, and there is no shifting dullness. Extremities are warm with radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses 2+/4 bilaterally, no cyanosis, clubbing, or edema. Musculoskeletal survey demonstrates full active range of motion of metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints; there is mild ulnar deviation at the second and third MCPs but no synovitis, effusion, or tendon friction rubs. Neurologic screening shows cranial nerves II-XII intact, strength 5/5 throughout, normal deep-tendon reflexes, preserved sensation to pinprick and vibration, and a smooth tandem gait. Skin inspection reveals faint hyperpigmentation over the malar areas and scattered healed acneiform scars, but no active discoid lesions, alopecia, oral ulcers, or livedo reticularis. Point-of-care laboratory tests obtained today show hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cells 5.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 248 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (baseline 3–6 mg/L for her). Twelve-lead electrocardiogram records normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 150 ms, QRS 90 ms, axis 25°, and no ST-segment deviation. She wishes advice on safe analgesic choices for the physically demanding externship, timing of hydroxychloroquine refills in a remote area, strategies to minimize stomach upset when field meals are irregular, and whether her mildly abnormal liver enzymes necessitate postponing travel.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weighted comorbidities; the age adjustment adds no points below age 50.
- Age 23: 0 points.
- Connective tissue disease: systemic lupus erythematosus qualifies even though it is controlled on hydroxychloroquine → 1 point.
- Peptic ulcer disease: the endoscopically confirmed duodenal ulcer counts despite subsequent healing → 1 point.
- Mild liver disease: persistent aminotransferase elevation attributed to hepatic inflammation, with preserved synthetic function and no portal hypertension → 1 point.
- No other qualifying comorbidity is documented → 0 points.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
